title: Hanukkah
lead: Hanukkah, "Dedication", is the eight-day Jewish feast beginning on the 25th of Kislev, which remembers the purification and rededication of the Temple by Judah Maccabee in 164 BC, three years after Antiochus IV had defiled it. It is kept by lighting lamps for eight nights.

sections.b: 1 Maccabees tells how Judah and his brothers cleansed the Temple, built a new altar, and dedicated it with sacrifices and songs on the 25th of Kislev, and ordered that the days of the dedication be kept every year for eight days with joy (1 Maccabees 4:36–59). 2 Maccabees adds that it was kept like the Feast of Booths, with thyrsi, branches and palms (2 Maccabees 1:9; 2 Maccabees 10:5–8). John's Gospel sets a scene in Jerusalem at "the Dedication" in winter (John 10:22). The Talmud tells the story of the single jar of pure oil that burned for eight days and sets the rules for the lights (Shabbat 21b–23a). Hanukkah is not one of the feasts of the law of Moses; like Purim, it was set up later to remember a deliverance.
